item.title: NVIDIA releases gds-diag tool to simplify GPUDirect Storage diagnostics
item.description:
NVIDIA releases gds-diag tool to simplify GPUDirect Storage diagnostics

NVIDIA has introduced gds‑diag, an open‑source command‑line utility (with an optional AI‑agent skill) that assesses environments, identifies problems, and suggests improvements for GPUDirect Storage deployments.

🔍 Overview

  • GPUDirect Storage (GDS) accelerates GPU storage access in on‑premises and cloud environments.
  • It provides a robust, portable, and efficient data path between NVIDIA GPUs and storage targets to increase bandwidth, minimize latency, and reduce CPU and memory utilization across a broad range of platforms, application frameworks, and workload patterns.
  • Configuring GDS starts with understanding your environment – which settings and storage paths are appropriate for your platform and workload?

🛠️ How gds‑diag works

  • Command‑line mode – a single Python script with multiple subcommands that focus on different diagnostic tasks.
  • AI‑agent mode – a natural‑language interface that interprets intent, selects and invokes the appropriate subcommands, and coordinates multi‑step diagnostic workflows.
  • The agent skill adds model‑guided reasoning: it can interpret diagnostic results, apply relevant system context, and propose or carry out appropriate remediation.
  • The tool runs on Linux systems with Python 3.8 or newer. NVIDIA datacenter‑class GPU and CUDA Toolkit 12.2 or newer are required for GDS itself, but they are not dependencies of gds‑diag.

🚀 Getting Started

  1. Clone the repository: git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/MagnumIO.git
  2. Choose a usage model:
    • Command‑line tool – deterministic, minimal‑dependency path.
    • AI agent – intuitive, flexible, natural‑language interaction (recommended when available).
  3. Open the gds-diag directory in your preferred AI coding assistant and follow the Agent skill usage guidance (if using the agent mode).
  4. Run ./gds-diag.py --help to browse subcommands, or run ./gds-diag.py all /path/to/check for an end‑to‑end diagnostic sequence.

📋 Diagnostic command categories

Category Example subcommand Purpose
End‑to‑end checks all Automatically selects appropriate diagnostics for your environment and runs them in sequence.
Preparing for installation pre-install Checks GPU support and CUDA Toolkit installation.
Storage planning support-matrix Views supported storage targets and helps plan your deployment.

The tool works in bare‑metal, virtual‑machine, and container environments.

📦 Availability

  • gds‑diag is bundled with the NVIDIA Magnum IO GitHub repository and has no additional dependencies to install.
  • It is validated with both Claude and Codex, and may work with other AI tools as well.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a robust, portable, and efficient data path for GPU‑centric workloads.
  • Reduces CPU and memory utilization while increasing bandwidth and lowering latency.
  • Offers both a deterministic command‑line experience and a flexible natural‑language agent, giving users multiple ways to optimize GDS deployments.

#NVIDIA #GPUDirectStorage #AIagents #Linux #Diagnostics

Source: How to Check and Configure NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage for Your Platform | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: GPU Fractioning Operator Enables Fine‑Grained GPU Sharing in Kubernetes
item.description:
GPU Fractioning Operator Enables Fine‑Grained GPU Sharing in Kubernetes

Many AI workloads need only a fraction of a GPU, and allocating a whole device to each workload can leave capacity idle. An open‑source Kubernetes operator called gpu‑fractioning now lets platform teams share GPUs at the memory and compute level, using new CUDA 13.4 enforcement features and NVIDIA’s existing sharing mechanisms.

🔍 Overview

  • AI workloads often require only part of a GPU’s memory and compute resources.
  • Sharing GPUs lets platform teams serve more workloads with the same hardware.
  • NVIDIA GPUs already support several sharing approaches: MIG, time‑slicing, and Multi‑Process Service (MPS).

🛠️ How it works

  • CUDA 13.4 memory enforcement: a workload requests a memory size; CUDA reserves it and rejects allocations that exceed the limit, giving the workload a guaranteed minimum and a maximum it can grow into when memory is free.
  • Compute modes: each workload can run in the default time‑sharing mode or choose the sm‑sharing mode (MPS) that runs processes concurrently in separate address spaces.
  • The enforcement logic runs on the node; it is independent of the scheduler that placed the workload.

⚙️ Key components

  • gpu‑fractioning operator (hosted under the KAI Scheduler GitHub organization) – sets up MPS on every GPU node, applies per‑workload memory limits and compute mode, and measures usage per fraction.
  • NVIDIA GPU Operator – provides the driver and container‑runtime setup; gpu‑fractioning runs alongside it.
  • Pod annotations – developers specify resource limits and compute mode in the pod YAML; the scheduler writes the chosen GPU slice and mode into per‑container annotations.
  • GPU Fractioning Operator – reads those annotations and configures the assigned GPUs to enforce the requested memory and compute settings.
  • KAI Scheduler – first scheduler integrated with gpu‑fractioning; from version v0.18.0 it offers a sharing mode called NvFractions that selects a slice of a GPU for each workload and writes the required annotations.

🚀 Availability

  • The gpu‑fractioning operator is open source and lives on GitHub under the KAI Scheduler organization.
  • It works with any Kubernetes scheduler capable of writing the required annotations; KAI Scheduler is the reference implementation.
  • Starting with KAI Scheduler v0.18.0, the NvFractions mode is available out‑of‑the‑box.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables multiple AI workloads to run on a single GPU without idle capacity.
  • Provides transparent memory enforcement and optional compute sharing modes.
  • Allows administrators to choose the sharing strategy that best fits their cluster.

GPU sharing techniques in NVIDIA GPUs

Technique Key property
Multi‑Instance GPU (MIG) Splits a GPU into hardware‑isolated instances that are transparent to the application
Time‑slicing Lets several processes take turns without memory enforcement
Multi‑Process Service (MPS) – sm‑sharing Runs processes concurrently in separate address spaces

#GPUSharing #Kubernetes #CUDA #AIWorkloads

Source: Memory-Enforced GPU Sharing in Kubernetes with NVIDIA CUDA 13.4 | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA KvikIO Python Library Demonstrates Direct GPU Storage Access via GPUDirect Storage
item.description:
NVIDIA KvikIO Python Library Demonstrates Direct GPU Storage Access via GPUDirect Storage

NVIDIA’s Magnum IO GPUDirect Storage (GDS) now works with the KvikIO Python library to let AI applications move data directly from storage into GPU memory, bypassing the CPU.

🔍 Overview

  • GPU applications are processing ever‑growing datasets with increasingly powerful accelerators.
  • The 2025 Stanford AI Index reports that compute for notable AI models has been doubling roughly every five months, while the size of datasets used to train LLMs has been doubling roughly every eight months.
  • As computation and data scale together, moving data efficiently from storage becomes a necessity for keeping accelerators supplied.
  • NVIDIA Magnum IO GPUDirect Storage (GDS) addresses this challenge by enabling a direct data path between supported storage and GPU memory.
  • The direct path avoids unnecessary staging through CPU memory and reduces overall CPU utilization in the system.
  • GDS is supported by a growing ecosystem that includes many major storage vendors.
  • At the application layer, Python plays a central role in modern AI development; as of August 2025, nearly half of all new AI projects on GitHub were built primarily in Python.

🧩 How It Works

Component Role
GPUDirect Storage (GDS) Enables a direct data path between supported storage and GPU memory.
cuFile C library and API through which applications and frameworks access GDS.
KvikIO Python and C++ library that sits above cuFile, providing high‑level, idiomatic interfaces and additional controls over how I/O requests are performed.
  • The application supplies a file‑system path and a GPU buffer.
  • KvikIO decides whether to route the request through cuFile (direct path) or use its POSIX compatibility path, which stages data through host memory.
  • When cuFile is selected, KvikIO registers the file and issues the I/O using the target GPU buffer.
  • cuFile then determines the actual transfer path based on system support, the file system, and its configuration; it may use the accelerated GDS path or fall back to a CPU‑staged compatibility path.
  • Reaching the cuFile API confirms that KvikIO selected cuFile, but does not by itself confirm that the accelerated GDS path was activated.

⚙️ Tutorial Highlights

  • Demonstrates how to use the NVIDIA KvikIO Python API to configure storage I/O, read data into GPU memory, and confirm that the accelerated path within GDS was activated.
  • Shows how to inspect KvikIO and cuFile settings that influence the path each operation takes.
  • Tested on an x86_64 system with an NVIDIA H100 GPU, CUDA 13.3, and cuFile 1.18.
  • The system used a local NVMe device formatted with ext4; a PIX connection between the GPU and NVMe device means the path traverses at most one PCIe bridge.
  • IOMMU and ACS were disabled to preserve PCIe peer‑to‑peer transfers, and the nvidia-fs kernel module was loaded to provide the accelerated path.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Doubling compute and dataset sizes increase pressure on the storage‑to‑GPU data pipeline.
  • Direct storage‑to‑GPU transfers reduce CPU overhead, freeing CPU resources for other parts of the AI workload.
  • Providing a high‑level Python interface (KvikIO) aligns with the fact that nearly half of new AI projects are Python‑centric, lowering the barrier for developers to adopt accelerated I/O.
  • A growing storage‑vendor ecosystem around GDS broadens hardware compatibility for future AI systems.

#NVIDIA #GPUDirectStorage #KvikIO #AI #Python

Source: How to Read Data into GPU Memory in Python with NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: TorchNeuron Model Support Space Shows Which Transformers Run on AWS Trainium
item.description:
TorchNeuron Model Support Space Shows Which Transformers Run on AWS Trainium

🔍 Overview

A new Hugging Face Space, torch‑neuronx‑model‑support, lets you see whether a given Transformers model runs unmodified on AWS Trainium and provides the exact script to run it yourself.

🛠️ How it works

  • Uses the torch‑neuronx package, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium.
  • Runs Transformers models on Trainium the same way they run on any other device.
  • The provided run.py script loads the model with from_pretrained, shards it when needed, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

📊 What the Space displays

  • PASS/FAIL result for each model.
  • Number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over.
  • Wall‑time of the run (compilation included).
  • Peak device memory usage.
  • The Neuron stack version, required packages, and the run.py script used.
  • If a model is omitted, the Space explains why (e.g., not prioritized or truly incompatible).

📈 Testing methodology

  • Tests run on a Trainium2 (trn2) instance, typically in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container.
  • Each model is sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights (maximum 16 cores, i.e., four Trainium2 devices).
  • Most models use tensor parallelism; Mixture‑of‑Experts models without a tensor‑parallel plan use expert parallelism only.
  • The test generates 32 tokens and checks them.
    • On a single core, the tokens are compared with a CPU run of the same checkpoint.
    • When sharded, a small judge model verifies that the text is fluent English.
  • A PASS only confirms correctness of the 32‑token output; it says nothing about throughput or longer generations.

⚙️ Configurability

  • The Space opens on the Selected view (our own selection of top‑downloaded and trending models).
  • You can switch to Trending or Downloads views and type part of a model name to look it up.
  • Versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx‑cc) and Transformers library can be chosen.
  • When a model is left out on purpose, the Space tells you the reason.

📌 Current scope

  • Only Transformers models are tested.
  • The selection is limited to text‑generation and image‑text‑to‑text models.
  • Only models that fit on four Trainium2 devices (up to 16 cores) are included.

🚀 Getting started

  1. Open the Space (it starts on the Selected view).
  2. Choose the desired neuronx‑cc and Transformers versions.
  3. Follow the displayed run.py script: install the listed packages, then run on a trn2 instance.
  4. The first run compiles the model’s graphs; subsequent runs can reuse compiled graphs by copying them from the public NEFF cache bucket.

🔎 Where the data comes from

  • All rows are sourced from the public aws‑neuron/torch‑neuronx‑model‑support dataset.
  • The dataset contains one Parquet file per pair of neuronx‑cc and library versions.
  • Each row stores the model’s result, any error, the stack versions, and the run.py script that was executed.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

#TorchNeuron #AWS #Trainium #Transformers #ModelSupport

Source: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

item.title: Training Qwen3 on a Single AWS Trainium2 Instance with TorchNeuron and NKI MoE
item.description:
Training Qwen3 on a Single AWS Trainium2 Instance with TorchNeuron and NKI MoE

This post demonstrates three ways to train the Qwen‑3 model on a single AWS trn2.48xlarge instance equipped with Trainium2 accelerators, using TorchNeuron, torchtitan‑neuron and optional NKI mixture‑of‑experts kernels.

🔍 Overview

  • TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device, enabling torchtitan to use it through standard PyTorch interfaces.
  • When torch_neuronx is installed, TorchNeuron registers the Trainium device and torchtitan detects it at startup.
  • The walkthrough runs on a single trn2.48xlarge instance (16 Trainium2 accelerators, 128 physical NeuronCores, 64 logical NeuronCores at LNC=2).

⚙️ Environment

Component Version
torch 2.14.0
torch_neuronx 2.14.3
transformers 5.16.0
torchtitan‑neuron release‑2.33 (0.2.2+neuron.1)
Instance trn2.48xlarge (16 Trainium2, 128 physical NeuronCores, 64 logical NeuronCores)

🚀 Training Configurations

1️⃣ Transformers v5 backend

  • Uses AutoModelForCausalLM to load Hub models and reads/writes published safetensors.
  • Launches 64 training processes, one per logical NeuronCore.
  • Data‑parallel sharding across all 64 ranks.
  • Saves final checkpoint as Hugging Face safetensors.
  • Example result for Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507:
    • Step‑1 loss 6.54 from published weights.
    • Step‑1 loss 12.43 from random initialization.

2️⃣ torchtitan native Qwen3Model

  • Switches to torchtitan’s native implementation by changing config.model_spec.
  • model_registry("4B", attn_backend="sdpa") selects the native Qwen3 model with scaled dot‑product attention (SDPA).

3️⃣ NKI Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) kernels

  • Adds Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) MoE kernels from the torchtitan‑neuron recipes.
  • Uses torchtitan’s override registry to attach the custom kernel.
  • qwen3_nki_moe_config() replaces the MoE block with the NKI grouped‑experts implementation, selects SDPA and a gather‑free rotary embedding.
  • Configuration details:
    • Data‑parallel sharding across 64 ranks, tensor‑parallel degree 1.
    • num_experts=64 sets the number of experts (not the expert‑parallel degree).
    • CompileConfig(enable=False) runs the example in eager mode.
  • TorchNeuron supports the registered NKI operators in both eager execution and torch.compile modes.

🧩 Execution Modes

  • Eager mode: Neuron compiles operations as they execute.
  • torch.compile: Neuron compiles the captured graph.

📚 Getting Started

  • Use a single trn2.48xlarge with either the AWS Deep Learning AMI for Neuron or a Neuron PyTorch training container.
  • Install torch_neuronx to enable device registration and torchtitan detection.

💡 Why it Matters

  • Demonstrates that a single Trainium2‑powered instance can train a 4‑billion‑parameter LLM using standard PyTorch interfaces.
  • Shows flexibility: the same hardware can run a Hugging Face Transformers backend, a native torchtitan implementation, or custom NKI MoE kernels without changing the underlying instance.
  • Provides a reproducible recipe for researchers and engineers to explore performance trade‑offs between eager execution, graph compilation, and custom kernel extensions.

#Trainium #TorchNeuron #Qwen3 #MoE #Neuron

Source: Train Qwen3 on AWS Trainium with torchtitan | Amazon Web Services

item.title: PyTorch 2.15 Enhancements for Metal Performance Shaders on Mac
item.description:
PyTorch 2.15 Enhancements for Metal Performance Shaders on Mac

PyTorch 2.15 introduces significant performance and memory optimizations for Apple silicon Macs via Metal Performance Shaders (MPS), specifically targeting Large Language Model (LLM) decoding, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, and video processing.

💡 Why it matters

Performance gains are most evident in MoE models, which decode 5–6.5× faster than in version 2.14. For example, on an M3 Ultra using torch.compile:

Model 2.14 Speed PyTorch 2.15 Speed
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 9.4 tokens/s 61.3 tokens/s
LFM2.5-8B-A1B 23.6 tokens/s 123.6 tokens/s

🧩 How it works

  • FP8 Support: PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS. These use one byte per value, requiring half the storage of BF16 or FP16. Tensors can be multiplied directly on the GPU using F.scaled_mm, which supports rowwise and tensorwise scaling.
  • MoE Optimizations: New Metal kernels read group offsets directly on the GPU using Metal Performance Primitives or a separate Metal path, replacing the 2.14 method of copying offsets to the CPU. A dedicated decoding path and specialized kernels for small groups further reduce GPU-CPU syncs and improve top-k routing.
  • Linear Layer Improvements: F.linear now connects to GEMV kernels for common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding inputs with fused bias additions. This resulted in a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models.
  • General GPU Acceleration: Softmax over the vocabulary is approximately 8× faster, and there is increased GPU support for complex LU and triangular solves, QR decomposition, and small-matrix inverses.

⚙️ Key details

  • Video and Audio: Faster paths are available for reductions, interpolation backward, dropout, padding, convolutions, and audio/video training.
  • Memory Efficiency: Wan2.2’s tiled VAE video decode memory peak has been reduced from 270 GiB to approximately 8 GiB.
  • Bug Fixes: A padding change fixes an issue where the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder corrupted images on MPS. Encode-decode round trips now match CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB.
  • Python Control: Users now have access to public MPS streams and more reliable event timing.

🚀 Availability

  • System Requirements: Apple silicon Mac running macOS 15 or later.
  • Software Requirements: PyTorch 2.15 requires Python 3.11 or later.
  • Diagnostics: The MPS availability check now specifies the reason if the OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available.

🔍 Looking Ahead

PyTorch 2.16 is expected to bring faster LLM decoding, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations, and attention fully implemented on Metal.

#PyTorch #AppleSilicon #Metal #LLM #MachineLearning

Source: MPS in PyTorch 2.15

item.title: TorchTPU Brings Native PyTorch Support to Google Cloud TPUs
item.description:
TorchTPU Brings Native PyTorch Support to Google Cloud TPUs

With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. The integration lets Transformers, Diffusers and custom kernels run natively on Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs).

🔍 Overview

  • TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit and is Google’s own AI accelerator.\
  • Google has been designing TPUs for about ten years and uses them for its models, including Gemini.\
  • TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.

🧩 How it works

  • TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch.\
  • It includes Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for extra speed.\
  • TPU kernels are written in Pallas, giving low‑level hardware control.\
  • Additional kernels can be imported from the Tokamax library.\
  • Installation on a TPU VM is a single command: 
    1

    pip install torch-tpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
  • To load a model on a TPU, set device_map="tpu".\
  • The TensorParallelConfig can be passed to from_pretrained to shard the model across chips, so the full model never has to fit in one place.

⚙️ Key details

  • Transformers v5 is built to be the source of truth for model definitions, enabling them to run anywhere, including TPUs.\
  • Diffusers now treats TPU as a first‑class device.\
  • Example runs on a Cloud TPU v6e‑4 with 4 chips (TP=4), bf16 precision, batch size 1.\
  • At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3‑30B‑A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B‑A4B.\
  • Decode throughput comparisons on a TPU v6e‑8 show Hub kernels outperforming the default implementation.

🚀 Availability

  • The Kernels Hub provides ready‑to‑use TPU kernels.\
  • TorchTPU is publicly installable via pip.\
  • A nightly CI on TPU is being added, with results to appear in the Transformers dashboard.

💡 Why it matters

  • By making TPU a first‑class device in PyTorch, developers can train and serve large language models on Google Cloud without rewriting code.\
  • Sharding with TensorParallelConfig removes the need for a single device to hold the entire model, enabling very large models to run on TPU pods.

Component Summary

Component Role
TorchTPU Adds TPU as a PyTorch backend
Pallas kernels Tuned TPU kernels, low‑level control
Tokamax library Additional kernels that can be imported

#PyTorch #TPU #TorchTPU #Transformers #Diffusers

Source: Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

item.title: Fused MoE Kernel Optimizes Decode Performance on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs
item.description:
Fused MoE Kernel Optimizes Decode Performance on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs

Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) models boost LLM capacity while keeping per‑token compute low, but the decode phase suffers from high latency because the underlying GPU kernels are inefficient.

🔍 Overview

  • MoE is a sparsely‑activated architecture that scales large language model capacity while keeping per‑token compute low.
  • MoE operations make up a large share of total compute time, so inefficiencies directly raise request latency and cost.
  • Optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains.

🧩 How MoE and Fused Kernels Work

  • Fused MoE merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched GPU operation, replacing separate sequential loop operations.
  • This fusion provides latency advantages but adds complexity to kernel implementation and debugging.

⚙️ Hopper WGMMA Constraints

  • NVIDIA Hopper uses the Warp Group Matrix Multiply‑Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction, executed across a cooperative warp‑group of 128 threads.
  • In the wgmma.mma_async definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension M to 64, defining the thread‑mapping topology.
  • Operand A must occupy this fixed M = 64 dimension (using registers or shared memory); Operand B occupies the variable N dimension via a shared‑memory descriptor.
  • The operand slots are structurally non‑interchangeable, and peak tile utilization requires M ≥ 64.
  • The hardware enforces a minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 rows.

Table: Operand Mapping on Hopper WGMMA

Operand Fixed/Variable Dimension Mapping Requirement
A Fixed M = 64 rows Must fill a 64‑row layout bucket
B Variable N dimension Can be large (e.g., 8192)

📈 Decoding Bottleneck and the Flip Technique

  • Decode processes a single token per user sequence, yielding a thin batch dimension M (often M < 64, sometimes M = 1).
  • Matrix A becomes a thin vector (e.g., 1 × 4096), while matrix B (expert weights) remains a large dense block (e.g., 4096 × 8192).
  • Because M is tiny, A cannot fill the hardware’s 64‑row layout, leaving many Tensor Core lanes idle and causing poor utilization.
  • MoE layers fracture the workload across many experts, making them especially sensitive to these constraints.
  • For a topk=8 routine, the effective N dimension inside the fused kernel expands to tens or hundreds of thousands of parameters.
  • Flipping the multiplication (transposing the matrices before PTX assembly) moves the large expert dimension N = 8192 into the first operand position, satisfying the mandatory 64‑row requirement and unlocking hardware prefetching.
  • This re‑alignment matches the exact topography of Hopper silicon, allowing the expansive N dimension to flood the required rows and dramatically improve hardware utilization.

💡 Why It Matters

  • By addressing the structural asymmetry of Hopper’s WGMMA instruction, the fused MoE kernel reduces decode latency.
  • Better utilization of Tensor Core capacity lowers the compute cost of serving MoE‑based LLMs.
  • The technique enables MoE models to retain their capacity‑scaling benefits without incurring prohibitive inference overhead.

#MixtureOfExperts #HopperGPU #KernelOptimization #LLMInference

Source: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services

item.title: NVIDIA Announces cuObject General Availability and Expands xio-sig Partnership
item.description:
NVIDIA Announces cuObject General Availability and Expands xio-sig Partnership

NVIDIA has announced the general availability of cuObject client and server libraries and is expanding xio-sig to include cuObject alongside cuFile in partnership with Microsoft and Google Cloud.

🧩 How it works

SCADA serves as the software infrastructure supporting high-throughput, fine-grained, GPU-initiated storage access. This system enables compute accelerators—including GPUs, TPUs, and XPUs—to utilize remote direct memory access (RDMA) via NIC- or DPU-accelerated data transfers, such as NVIDIA ConnectX NIC or NVIDIA BlueField DPU.

This architecture allows AI accelerators to access file and object storage without routing data through the server CPU, resulting in:

  • Higher throughput
  • Lower latency
  • Reduced CPU utilization for data reads and writes

⚙️ Key details

Through the NVIDIA Storage-Next initiative, NVIDIA is leading a group of over 40 vendors and customers—including hyperscalers, application developers, controller vendors, NAND vendors, and storage providers—to define GPU-driven storage and establish interoperable, open industry standards.

Component Function
cuObject Provides APIs and an RDMA wire protocol for building accelerated object-storage applications and servers.
xio-sig Provides a path for the cuObject client to interoperate with any server-side implementation adhering to the wire protocol.
SCADA Server SDK Enables storage providers to build servers that respond to GPU-initiated requests from SCADA clients.
Storage Lender Service Part of the effort accompanying the SCADA command-line utility for configuration and deployment.

💡 Why it matters

The general availability of cuObject libraries offers standardized methods for accelerated AI data access using both object and file protocols for storage consumers, storage providers, open source framework developers, and AI application developers.

Interoperability efforts include:

  • IBM: Demonstrated a prototype integrating SCADA and IBM Storage Scale, where a SCADA client sends requests to a Storage Scale SCADA server built with the new SDK.
  • Google Cloud: A maintainer for cuFile in xio-sig, Google Cloud is evaluating expanding its participation for cuObject.
  • Microsoft: Planning to join the xio-sig Board to improve storage I/O interoperability.

🚀 Availability

  • cuObject client and server libraries are generally available.
  • cuObject Server 2.0.0 and NVIDIA CUDA 13.4 preview downloads are available.
  • Repository structures are established for cuFile and cuObject; headers, the cuObject wire protocol, and library implementation code (libxFile and xFilekernel) will be shared after the production-ready stack passes conformance tests.
  • Governance documents are currently under review by pending Board Members.

#NVIDIA #GPU #ObjectStorage #RDMA #cuObject

Source: Expanding AI Storage Access with NVIDIA cuObject and the NVIDIA SCADA Server SDK | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA Transformer Engine Optimizations for Mixture-of-Experts Architectures
item.description:
NVIDIA Transformer Engine Optimizations for Mixture-of-Experts Architectures

NVIDIA has updated the Transformer Engine (TE) to address bottlenecks in Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures through optimized primitives, kernel fusion, and low-precision training.

🔍 Overview

MoE models scale by replacing a single dense feed-forward block with multiple expert networks. These architectures use many subnetworks, or experts, while activating only a small subset for each token.

🧩 How it works

While baseline Hugging Face implementations iterate over experts in a Python loop—triggering separate kernel launches for each—the Transformer Engine introduces several optimizations:

  • GroupedLinear: Applies multiple linear transformations in a single call by gathering input tokens and expert weights. It accepts per-expert token counts (split_sizes) and uses the TE grouped GEMM path to reduce scheduling and launch overhead.
  • GroupedMLP Kernel: Fuses GroupedLinear with routing-weight scaling, activation, MXFP8 quantization, and intermediate data movement.
  • ScaledSwiGLU: Combines expert feed-forward network computations with routing probabilities (scales).

⚙️ Key details

Feature Function
MXFP8 Reduces memory use by representing weights and activations with 8 bits and assigning a scaling factor to blocks of 32 consecutive values.
TE Autocast API Enables MXFP8 precision for forward and backward passes and folds dequantization into the fused path.
Quantization Converts BF16 weights and activations to MXFP8 before low-precision GEMM.
Dequantization Converts the result back to a higher-precision format.

🚀 Availability

  • Hardware: At least two GPUs are required for expert parallelism. The fused MXFP8 GroupedMLP kernel requires NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, which provide hardware acceleration for MXFP8 GEMMs via specialized Tensor Core instructions.
  • Implementation: The BioNeMo recipe utilizes TE to support FP8 and MXFP8 training.
  • Precision: The model retains its master weights in 16 bits (BF16).

💡 Why it matters

By replacing 16-bit BF16 representations with 8-bit formats (FP8 and MXFP8), the Transformer Engine reduces memory use while preserving numerical range and accuracy.

#NVIDIA #TransformerEngine #MoE #Blackwell #MachineLearning

Source: Efficient MoE Training for Biological Foundation Models | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: SymbolicLight V2 Hybrid Neuromorphic Architecture Improves FPGA Decode Throughput
item.description:
SymbolicLight V2 Hybrid Neuromorphic Architecture Improves FPGA Decode Throughput

SymbolicLight V2 is a new hybrid neuromorphic language architecture that combines continuous-state processing with sparse event computation.

🧩 How it works

Extending the spike-gated dual paths found in V1, SymbolicLight V2 introduces:

  • Graded signed events at further projections
  • Softmax-free local attention

⚙️ Key details

The 194M-parameter model was implemented across two different hardware environments:

Hardware Implementation Detail
Alveo U50C FPGA Digital fixed-point arithmetic
ARM CPU (ROCK 5T) Sparse integer execution on four Cortex-A76 cores

💡 Why it matters

Technical evaluations of the FPGA implementation at 175 MHz demonstrate that active-row weight gathering and valid-state KV loading improve performance:

  • Throughput: Decode throughput increased from 474.6 to 643.2 tokens/s (for a 32-token prefix and 128 outputs).
  • Energy Efficiency: Gross card energy per generated token fell from 0.06087 to 0.04407 J, a 27.6% reduction. Complete-request energy fell by 24.4-27.7% across three prefix lengths.
  • GPU Comparison: During short-context decode, integer FPGA execution used 89.1% less estimated card energy than a recorded RTX 5090 compiled-FP32 baseline, though arithmetic precisions differ and the GPU was not the lowest-energy tested configuration.
  • CPU Performance: On the ROCK 5T, complete requests reached 65.4 tokens/s at 9.80 W and 0.151 J per generated token at the adapter’s AC input.

An independent idle split attributed 82.8% of gross card energy to loaded idle, which explains the benefit of shorter token latency. These results connect event sparsity to omitted computation and data movement.

Note on quality: Evaluation held the deployed checkpoint fixed; its quality trails a same-budget dense control, meaning these results do not establish equal-quality efficiency.

#NeuromorphicComputing #FPGA #LLM #EnergyEfficiency

Source: SymbolicLight V2: Hybrid Neuromorphic Architecture and Sparse Execution for Low-Energy Language Inference
